goal: Make EnableRateLimit=false actually disable the rate limiter, independent of APIRateLimitPerMinute's value, so the two names mean what they say: EnableRateLimit is the master switch, APIRateLimitPerMinute is the threshold.

steps: 1. In internal/server/server_lifecycle.go, change the condition that builds the real limiter (around L1402) from `if rpm := config.AppConfig.APIRateLimitPerMinute; rpm > 0 {` to `if config.AppConfig.EnableRateLimit; rpm := config.AppConfig.APIRateLimitPerMinute; rpm > 0 {` — i.e. require BOTH EnableRateLimit==true AND rpm>0 (Go doesn't support that exact multi-clause `if` syntax; write it as `if config.AppConfig.EnableRateLimit && config.AppConfig.APIRateLimitPerMinute > 0 { rpm := config.AppConfig.APIRateLimitPerMinute; ... }`).

title: Determine whether the persistent UI lockup is backend (slow/unbounded requests) or frontend (rendering/virtualization), with evidence, before writing any fix
verdict_evidence: The item explicitly demands this exact investigation sequence ('State which of the two it is, with evidence, before writing any fix') and gives concrete already-measured backend evidence from the same night (36s for a 1-row request, 2m10s for a personalized-library endpoint, 4 OOM kills in 90 minutes, a 568s memdb warmup, 30 goroutines pinning 30GB from abandoned activity-log scans) that already strongly suggests a backend cause distinct from the DOM-volume hypothesis the previous round closed against — but the item still requires re-confirming this specific incident wasn't purely a warmup-window artifact before concluding.

why_tier: A structured reproduce-and-classify investigation (DevTools Network open, correlate with server logs/restart windows) with a clear decision tree already given by the item — bounded, but requires live reproduction against a running instance, not pure static analysis.
goal: Reproduce the reported lockup with browser DevTools Network open and classify it: are the slow-to-render views waiting on PENDING network requests (backend-bound), or are requests returning promptly while the page itself janks (frontend-bound)? If backend: identify the specific slow/unbounded endpoint(s) among the already-known-unbounded candidates in this codebase (the activity-log query ignoring client disconnect, described in this same night's findings, is a leading candidate — cross-reference L1970 in this scope, which is the tracked fix for exactly that). If frontend: profile whether virtualization is actually active on the specific list that janks, or only on a previously-fixed one. Separately, check whether the lockup correlates with the ~10-minute post-restart memdb-warmup window, since that would point at startup sequencing rather than either a backend request-handling bug or a frontend rendering bug.
background: Already measured on prod the same night (2026-08-11): GET /api/v1/audiobooks?library_state=imported&limit=1 took 36 seconds for one row; GET /api/libraries/{id}/personalized took 2m10s; the server was OOM-killed 4 times in 90 minutes; memdb warmup takes 568s during which 'library list warm-up: memdb not ready after 5 min, skipping' fires because warmup outlives its own waiter, so the list cache never warms; 30 abandoned-activity-log-query goroutines were found pinning 30GB with zero clients connected.

The previous round of this same UI-lockup investigation was closed against a DOM-volume/virtualization hypothesis — this item explicitly asks to state whether that hypothesis still holds or was wrong/no-longer-binding, rather than silently assuming virtualization work is still the right lever.
steps: 1. Reproduce the reported freeze with browser DevTools Network tab open, on both a freshly-restarted server (within the ~10min warmup window) and a warmed-up one, to separate startup-sequencing from a steady-state bug.

2. Record whether the janking view's requests are PENDING (not yet returned) at the time the page appears frozen, vs. returning quickly while the render itself stalls — this single observation is the item's primary decision fork.

3. If backend-bound: identify which endpoint(s) are slow, and check whether they match already-known-unbounded patterns in this codebase — specifically the activity-log query's client-disconnect-ignoring behavior (the item names this explicitly; cross-reference internal/server/maintenance_fixups.go and the activity Query path, and note whether L1970/L1957 in this same scope's fixes would address it).

4. If frontend-bound: use the React DevTools Profiler (or the browser Performance panel) to confirm whether virtualization (react-window or similar) is actually mounted and active on the SPECIFIC list component that janks in this reproduction, versus only on whichever list was fixed in a previous round — a regression where a NEW unvirtualized list was added since the last fix is a plausible explanation worth explicitly ruling in or out.

5. Check correlation with server restart/warmup timing: if the freeze reliably occurs only within ~10 minutes of a server restart, state this explicitly as the primary finding (startup sequencing) rather than as a footnote, since it would redirect the fix toward warmup-sequencing work rather than either frontend or steady-state backend work.

6. Write up the finding explicitly stating which of the three (backend steady-state, frontend rendering, warmup-window sequencing) is the binding constraint, with the DevTools/Profiler evidence, before any fix is written.
